HAEMATOLOGY__Foundations of Haematology:
Overview — Coagulation Cascade & Clotting Tests
The coagulation cascade = a sequence of clotting factor activations (secondary haemostasis) that converges on thrombin, which turns fibrinogen → fibrin to stabilise the platelet plug. The exam skill = mapping the three pathways to the two clotting tests (PT and APTT) and reading the pattern.
The spine
Intrinsic (APTT) + Extrinsic (PT) → Common pathway → thrombin → fibrin. Then map deficiencies/drugs onto whichever test is prolonged.
Cross-ref: Haemophilia / VWD (intrinsic, ↑APTT), DIC (everything consumed), blood transfusion products (FFP/cryo replace factors), anticoagulation (warfarin/heparin/DOAC targets).
Primary vs Secondary Haemostasis — the context
Primary haemostasis
Platelet plug — vessel injury → vWF binds platelets to exposed collagen → platelet activation/aggregation. Tested by platelet count + bleeding time/PFA.
Secondary haemostasis
The coagulation cascade — clotting factors generate fibrin to stabilise the plug. Tested by PT + APTT.
vWF bridges the two: it mediates platelet adhesion (primary) and carries factor VIII (secondary) — which is why VWD can prolong the APTT.

Overview — Haemostasis
Haemostasis = the process that stops bleeding after vessel injury, balanced against keeping blood flowing — the pro-clotting vs anti-clotting equilibrium.
The three stages: primary (platelet plug) → secondary (coagulation cascade → fibrin) → fibrinolysis (controlled breakdown).
Why it matters: explains bleeding disorders (platelet vs clotting factor), antiplatelets, and the bleeding-time vs clotting-time distinction — cross-ref the coagulation cascade subtab (secondary haemostasis), bleeding disorders, antiplatelets, DIC.

Overview — Natural Anticoagulant System
Clotting must be localised to the injury and switched off once the job is done — otherwise a clot would propagate through the whole vasculature. The natural anticoagulant system is the body's built-in brake on coagulation.
The organising principle: haemostasis is a balance between pro-coagulant (the cascade) and anti-coagulant forces; these natural anticoagulants keep the cascade in check — and losing them tips the balance toward thrombosis (thrombophilia).
Why it matters: explains the inherited thrombophilias (factor V Leiden, protein C/S/antithrombin deficiency), how heparin works, the nephrotic-syndrome VTE risk, and warfarin-induced skin necrosis — cross-ref the coagulation cascade + haemostasis subtabs, anticoagulation, nephrotic syndrome, VTE.
Why the Brake Is Needed — the context
The coagulation cascade is a powerful amplifying system (a small trigger → massive thrombin/fibrin generation), so it needs equally powerful off-switches to:
  • Localise the clot to the site of injury (not spread)
  • Limit its size
  • Remove it once healing occurs (overlaps with fibrinolysis)
The balance concept: at any moment, pro-coagulant and anti-coagulant forces are in equilibrium — tip toward pro-coagulant → thrombosis; tip toward anti-coagulant → bleeding.

The heparin link (key payoff): heparin (and LMWH) work by massively potentiating antithrombin III — heparin binds ATIII and accelerates its action ~1000-fold.

  • Acquired ATIII loss — nephrotic syndrome: ATIII lost in the urine → hypercoagulable → the VTE risk noted in the nephrotic syndrome topic (the cross-reference loop)
Protein C & Protein S — the warfarin / factor V Leiden link (high-yield)
Mechanism: thrombin (bound to thrombomodulin on intact endothelium) activates protein C → activated protein C (APC), with protein S as cofactor, inactivates factors Va and VIIIa → shuts down the cascade's amplification.
The elegant feedback: thrombin (the main clotting product) also triggers its own brake (via protein C) when it reaches healthy endothelium → the clot stays localised to the damaged area.
Both protein C and S are vitamin-K-dependent (like factors II, VII, IX, X) — the key to two high-yield clinical points:
Warfarin-induced skin necrosis
  • Warfarin lowers protein C faster than the clotting factors (shorter half-life) → a brief pro-thrombotic state at initiation → why you bridge with heparin when starting warfarin (cross-ref anticoagulation)
Factor V Leiden (commonest inherited thrombophilia)
  • A mutated factor V that resists inactivation by activated protein C ("APC resistance") → the brake cannot switch it off → thrombosis risk
Protein C or S deficiency (inherited thrombophilias): less brake → VTE risk.
The Endothelium's Role — the surface that keeps blood flowing
  • Intact endothelium is actively anti-thrombotic: produces prostacyclin + nitric oxide (inhibit platelet activation / vasodilate), expresses thrombomodulin (activates protein C), and heparan sulfate (ATIII cofactor)
  • Damaged/dysfunctional endothelium loses this → contributes to thrombosis (part of Virchow's triad)

Overview — Haematopoiesis
Haematopoiesis = the production of all blood cells from a common haematopoietic stem cell (HSC) in the bone marrow — a continuous, tightly-regulated process replacing billions of cells daily.
The organising principle: a single pluripotent stem cell differentiates down two main lineages — myeloid and lymphoid — and where the process fails or goes wrong defines the cytopenias, leukaemias, and marrow failure syndromes.
Why it matters: explains why marrow failure causes pancytopenia, how leukaemias arise (lineage + maturation block), why EPO treats CKD anaemia, and the basis of stem cell transplant — cross-ref red cell/haemoglobin physiology, anaemia, leukaemias, CKD (EPO), the immune cells.
Where It Happens — changes with age
  • Fetus: yolk sac → liver + spleen (mid-gestation) → bone marrow (late)
  • Children: all bones
  • Adults: the axial skeleton — vertebrae, sternum, ribs, pelvis, proximal femur/humerus (peripheral marrow becomes fatty)
  • Extramedullary haematopoiesis (liver/spleen reactivating) occurs in marrow stress/infiltration (e.g. myelofibrosis, thalassaemia) → hepatosplenomegaly

Overview — Red Cell Physiology & Haemoglobin
Red blood cells (erythrocytes) exist to carry oxygen (and help with CO₂) — their structure, haemoglobin content, and lifecycle are all specialised for that single job.
The organising principle: the red cell is a biconcave, anucleate bag of haemoglobin optimised for gas transport and deformability — and the anaemias/haemoglobinopathies are best understood as failures of production, structure, or haemoglobin.
Why it matters: underpins the anaemias (by size), haemoglobinopathies (sickle cell, thalassaemia), haemolysis, and the bilirubin/jaundice link — cross-ref haematopoiesis, O₂ dissociation curve, anaemia, sickle cell, thalassaemia, bilirubin metabolism.
Red Cell Structure — form fits function
  • Biconcave disc: maximises surface-area-to-volume for gas exchange + allows deformability (to squeeze through capillaries narrower than itself)
  • Anucleate (no nucleus/organelles in the mature cell): more room for haemoglobin + no mitochondria → relies on anaerobic glycolysis for energy (cannot use the O₂ it carries)
  • Flexible membrane (spectrin/ankyrin cytoskeleton): maintains shape + deformability → membrane defects cause abnormal shapes + haemolysis (e.g. hereditary spherocytosis)
  • Lifespan ~120 days: no nucleus → cannot repair → ages and is removed by the spleen (reticuloendothelial system)

📷 Image placeholder — Haemoglobin structure — 4 globin chains (2α + 2β in HbA), each with a haem group carrying a ferrous (Fe²⁺) iron and one O₂-binding site.

The iron point (high-yield): O₂ binds ferrous iron (Fe²⁺); if oxidised to ferric (Fe³⁺) → methaemoglobin, which cannot carry O₂ (methaemoglobinaemia).

Red Cell Metabolism — why it needs protection (high-yield)
No mitochondria → relies on glycolysis for ATP, plus two protective pathways:
Pentose phosphate pathway → G6PD
  • Produces NADPH → glutathione → protects against oxidative damage; G6PD is the key enzyme
  • G6PD deficiency → oxidative haemolysis (triggered by infection, fava beans, drugs e.g. primaquine/sulfonamides; Heinz bodies, bite cells) — ties to the malaria primaquine + drug ADR notes
Pyruvate kinase (glycolysis)
  • Generates ATP for the membrane; PK deficiency → haemolysis
The Red Cell Lifecycle — production to breakdown (links to jaundice)
📷 Image placeholder — Red cell breakdown / bilirubin pathway — splenic macrophages split Hb into recycled globin + iron and haem → biliverdin → unconjugated bilirubin → liver → bile.
  • Production (erythropoiesis): in marrow, driven by EPO (kidney), needs iron, B12, folate as building blocks → reticulocyte → mature RBC
  • Lifespan: ~120 days
Breakdown — the bilirubin link (high-yield)
  • Old/damaged RBCs removed by the spleen/macrophages → haemoglobin split into:
  • Globin → recycled to amino acids
  • Iron → recycled (stored as ferritin, transported by transferrin)
  • Haem → biliverdin → bilirubin → unconjugated bilirubin → liver conjugates it → bile
The haemolysis logic: ↑red cell breakdown → ↑unconjugated bilirubin (pre-hepatic jaundice) + ↑LDH + ↓haptoglobin + ↑reticulocytes → the lab picture of haemolysis.

Overview — White Cells & the Immune Cells
White cells (leucocytes) are the cellular immune defence, produced in the marrow and circulating in blood. This note covers them as blood cells: what each does, the FBC differential, and the clinical patterns (which cell rises in which situation).

Iron is absorbed in the duodenum and proximal jejunum. Gastric acid keeps iron in the soluble ferrous (Fe²⁺) form required for absorption via DMT-1. PPIs, post-gastrectomy, or H. pylori-related achlorhydria → Fe³⁺ (insoluble) → malabsorption.

"Empty shelves — more shopping trolleys sent out"

Hepcidin rises (acute phase reactant) → iron sequestered in macrophages → ↑ ferritin (stored away). Less transport needed → ↓ TIBC. Mechanism: starves bacteria of iron.

"Iron locked in the vault — no delivery trucks needed"

Hereditary Spherocytosis

Autosomal dominant — most common inherited haemolytic anaemia in Northern Europeans. Defect in RBC membrane proteins (spectrin, ankyrin, band 3) → sphere-shaped RBCs → fragile → destroyed in spleen.

Clinical: Jaundice, gallstones (pigment), splenomegaly, aplastic crisis (Parvovirus B19)

Investigations: Spherocytes on film • ↑ MCHC • ↑ Reticulocytes • Family history

Management: Folate supplementation (high turnover) + splenectomy (removes destruction site). Cholecystectomy if gallstones symptomatic.

Aplastic crisis: Parvovirus B19 suppresses erythropoiesis → sudden severe anaemia in patients with compensated haemolysis (because they rely on high reticulocyte output).

Same pathophysiology as spherocytosis but RBCs are ellipse-shaped. Usually milder. Same membrane protein defects. Blood film: elliptocytes.

X-linked recessive — more common in Mediterranean and Sub-Saharan African populations. G6PD enzyme prevents oxidative injury to RBCs (glutathione pathway). Without it, oxidative stress → denatured Hb (Heinz bodies) → RBC destruction.

HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Disease:
The decisive fork: HbS polymerises when deoxygenated. Deoxygenation → HbS polymerises → RBC sickles → two branches: (1) haemolysis (fragile RBC → anaemia, gallstones, folate demand, aplastic vulnerability) and (2) vaso-occlusion (rigid cell jams capillaries → infarcts, organ damage, crises). Every complication lives on one of these two branches. Cross-ref Thalassaemia: same β-chain, same chr 11, but qualitative defect here vs quantitative there.
Overview & Pathophysiology
What is sickle cell disease?
  • Haemoglobinopathy — autosomal recessive
  • Point mutation in β-globin (chr 11) → glutamate → valine at position 6 → HbS
  • Deoxy-HbS polymerises → RBC sickles; RBC lifespan 10–20 days (normal 120)
  • Sickling initially reversible on reoxygenation; becomes irreversible with repeated cycles → progressive organ damage
Epidemiology & genetics
  • Africa, Caribbean, India, Middle East
  • Heterozygote (trait) advantage — malaria protection → balanced polymorphism
  • Trait (HbAS): asymptomatic; trait NOT the same as disease (HbSS)
  • Antenatal + newborn heel-prick screening (day 5)
The two-branch spine: Haemolysis branch → anaemia, pigment gallstones, folate deficiency, aplastic crisis. Vaso-occlusion branch → stroke, ACS, AVN, priapism, CKD, retinopathy. Hyposplenism branch → functional asplenia → encapsulated-organism sepsis.

HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia:
The decisive fork: Which globin chain, and how many genes are affected? Alpha is graded by number of defective alleles (1→4); beta by trait vs non-transfusion-dependent vs transfusion-dependent. Everything — severity, presentation, transfusion-dependence — falls out of gene dosage. Cross-ref Anaemia note: thalassaemia is a key microcytic cause.
Overview
What is thalassaemia?
  • Haemoglobinopathy — autosomal recessive
  • Reduced or absent globin chain production
  • Defect: alpha (chromosome 16) or beta (chromosome 11)
The disease mechanism

Reduced production of one chain → excess of the paired chain → unstable precipitates → ineffective erythropoiesis + haemolysis → fragile RBCs → splenomegaly. It is the imbalance that causes disease.

Chr 11 mutation → reduced/absent beta chain → excess alpha chains precipitate → haemolysis + ineffective erythropoiesis.

  • Liver → cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma

Bone disease

  • Orthopaedic stabilisation for pathological fracture

  • Transfusion for symptomatic anaemia
  • Infection prophylaxis + vaccinations
  • Renal: avoid NSAIDs/nephrotoxins, dialysis if needed

  • Recurrent infections (immunoparesis)
  • Pathological fractures
  • Spinal cord compression
  • Hypercalcaemia

  • Renal failure (cast nephropathy)
  • Hyperviscosity syndrome
  • AL amyloid → cardiac, renal, peripheral neuropathy
  • Treatment-related neuropathy (bortezomib, thalidomide)

CRAB = the diagnostic tetrad. Its presence separates myeloma from MGUS/smouldering — the single most important discriminator.

Bence-Jones protein = urinary light chains. Urine dipstick is negative — dipstick detects albumin, not light chains. Must send urine electrophoresis.
Thalidomide → VTE — always co-prescribe aspirin or LMWH. A guaranteed MCQ trap.
Waldenström's = IgM variant; hyperviscosity not bone disease. Anaemia is normocytic normochromic; ESR and plasma viscosity raised.

Leukaemia = malignancy of haematopoietic stem cells → marrow replaced by clonal cells → other lineages suppressed (anaemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia)

Aetiology & Key Cytogenetics
Aetiology
  • Genetic change → clonal population

  • t(9;22) Philadelphia → BCR-ABL: >95% CML, some ALL → target with imatinib (TKI)

⚠ Tumour Lysis Syndrome

Presentation (Marrow Failure)

  • Bleeding/petechiae (↓platelets/thrombocytopenia)

  • FBC: ↓Hb, ↓platelets, WCC ↑ or ↓

  • MRD by flow cytometry guides relapse risk and de-escalation

AML
  • Age: predominantly >75y
  • Hallmark: Auer rods (pathognomonic)
  • ↑ risk after MDS or myeloproliferative disease
  • Chemo: cytarabine + daunorubicin
  • Transplant for intermediate/high-risk
  • APML subtype (~25y): t(15;17), associated with DIC (can worsen on treatment) → ATRA reverses bleeding and drives differentiation
ALL
  • Age: children (<5y) and >45y
  • Associations: Down's syndrome, EBV
  • CNS spread → LP + intrathecal methotrexate
  • Commonest childhood cancer
  • Chemo: vincristine, dexamethasone, asparaginase, daunorubicin; 2-year maintenance
  • Philadelphia+ ALL: add TKI (imatinib)
  • B-ALL monoclonals: rituximab (anti-CD20), blinatumomab (CD19/CD3)

Key Facts
  • Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) → BCR-ABL in >95%
  • Age ~65; middle-aged
  • Three phases: Chronic (~5 years, often incidental ↑WCC) → Accelerated → Blast crisis (>30% blasts, usually transforms to AML, often fatal)
Presentation
  • Insidious onset: fever, weight loss, sweats
  • Massive splenomegaly
  • Blood film: leucocytosis with myeloid precursors, basophilia

  • Imatinib (TKI — blocks BCR-ABL): first-line
  • Allogeneic SCT / interferon for advanced disease

Key Facts
  • Commonest leukaemia overall
  • Elderly patients (>55y); clonal mature B-cells; indolent but incurable
  • Blood film: smudge/smear cells
  • Immunophenotype: CD5, CD19, CD20, CD23

  • Often asymptomatic — incidental lymphocytosis on routine bloods
  • Later: marrow failure features, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly
  • AIHA (warm antibody — cross-ref haemolytic anaemia)

Management
  • Watch-and-wait (early/asymptomatic disease)
  • Symptomatic/progressive: FCR (fludarabine, cyclophosphamide, rituximab) — now largely second-line
  • Modern first-line: BTK inhibitors (ibrutinib/acalabrutinib) or venetoclax ± obinutuzumab

Aspirin all patients. Cytoreduction if high-risk: hydroxycarbamide, anagrelide, busulfan, interferon.

HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / Von Willebran:
The decisive fork: platelet-type vs coagulation-type bleeding. VWF sits at the platelet–vessel interface → mucocutaneous bleeding (gums, nose, periods) + prolonged bleeding time. Factors VIII/IX sit deep in the cascade → deep bleeding (joints, muscles) + prolonged APTT with normal bleeding time. VWD is the bridge: VWF carries factor VIII, so severe VWD can lower VIII and prolong APTT. Cross-ref DIC — acquired, consumptive, mixed clotting/bleeding.
The Two Disorders at a Glance
Von Willebrand Disease (VWD)
  • Commonest inherited bleeding disorder
  • Mostly autosomal dominant
  • Deficiency/dysfunction of VWF
  • Bleeding type: mucocutaneous
Haemophilia A & B
  • X-linked recessive — almost exclusively males
  • A = factor VIII deficiency; B = factor IX (Christmas disease)
  • Bleeding type: deep (haemarthroses, muscle)
VWF has two jobs: (1) platelet adhesion/aggregation at the vessel wall; (2) carrier and stabiliser of factor VIII. That dual role explains why severe VWD can produce haemophilia-like features (low VIII, ↑APTT).

VWF deficiency → defective platelet function + secondary factor VIII deficiency.

HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminated Intravasc:
The decisive fork: consumption. Massive coagulation activation consumes platelets and clotting factors faster than they are replaced — giving the paradox of clotting and bleeding simultaneously. Factors used up → PT/APTT/TT prolong; fibrinogen consumed → low; platelets consumed → thrombocytopenia; clots sheared in vessels → schistocytes; secondary fibrinolysis → ↑FDPs/D-dimer. DIC is always secondary — there is no primary DIC.
Overview
What is DIC?
  • Widespread intravascular fibrin generation from massive coagulation cascade activation
  • Core paradox: too much clotting and too little clotting simultaneously — microvascular thrombosis plus haemorrhage
  • Always secondary to an underlying trigger — never primary
Mechanism chain

Trigger → tissue factor exposed → coagulation cascade fires → fibrin + platelet consumption → secondary fibrinolysis → FDPs (which themselves worsen bleeding by inhibiting fibrin polymerisation) → haemorrhage + microvascular thrombosis

Aetiology

Unifying mechanism: anything that exposes or expresses tissue factor — endothelial damage, monocyte TF expression driven by cytokines, or direct TF release.

CategoryExamples
Sepsis (commonest)Gram-negative sepsis especially; cytokine-driven TF expression on monocytes
Trauma / tissue destructionBurns, major surgery, crush injury, fat embolism

HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusion Products:
Blood Products
Principle: Restrictive transfusion strategy (lower thresholds) → better outcomes. One unit at a time, then reassess.
Product Indication Key Facts
Red Cells
O neg = universal donor		 Anaemia / acute blood loss Non-ACS: transfuse if Hb <70, target 70–90 g/L
ACS: transfuse if Hb <80, target 80–100 g/L
Infuse over 90–120 min; stored at 4°C; use within 4h
FFP
AB = universal donor		 Clotting factor deficiency (PT/APTT >1.5× normal) Contains all clotting factors. Universal donor = AB (no anti-A or anti-B). Large volume — avoid in fluid overload.
Cryoprecipitate Low fibrinogen (<1.5 g/L) — DIC, liver failure, massive transfusion Concentrated: fibrinogen, factor VIII, vWF, factor XIII. Precipitate of FFP at 4°C → hence "cryo".
Platelets Severe thrombocytopenia with bleeding; prophylactic if <10×10⁹/L Stored at 20–24°C (NOT cold — cold causes aggregation). 1 adult dose ↑ platelet count ~20–30×10⁹/L.
PCC
Prothrombin Complex Concentrate		 Emergency warfarin reversal (major bleed, ICH, emergency surgery) Fastest reversal — within 1h. Contains factors II, VII, IX, X. Always give with IV vitamin K (factor VII short half-life → INR creeps back up).
Special Products
CMV-negative
For immunocompromised patients and neonates. CMV is leucocyte-transmitted — leucodepletion makes most products effectively CMV-safe, but seronegative products used for highest-risk (transplant, HIV, pregnancy).
Irradiated
T-cells in donor blood depleted by irradiation. Prevents TA-GVHD (Transfusion-Associated Graft-versus-Host Disease) — fatal in immunocompromised patients (haematology, stem cell transplant).
Transfusion Thresholds & Warfarin Reversal
Transfusion Thresholds
Non-ACS: transfuse if Hb <70 → target 70–90 g/L
ACS: transfuse if Hb <80 → target 80–100 g/L
Restrictive strategy (lower threshold) → fewer reactions, less fluid overload, better outcomes than liberal.
Warfarin Reversal
1. Stop warfarin
2. Vitamin K — IV (works in 4–6h) or oral (24h). Always give.
3. PCC — major bleed/ICH/emergency surgery. Reversal within 1h. Give WITH vitamin K.
4. FFP — older alternative; large volume, avoid in fluid overload.
Why K with PCC? Factor VII has a short half-life — without vitamin K, new factors won't be synthesised and INR will rebound.

Neutropenic Sepsis: Overview
MEDICAL EMERGENCY — commonest serious complication of chemotherapy, typically 7–14 days post-cycle (the nadir)

Definition (the diagnosis is a definition, not a judgement call):
Neutrophils <0.5 ×10⁹/L in a patient on anticancer treatment PLUS either temp >38°C or clinical signs of sepsis
⚠ Signs may be blunted — without neutrophils there is less inflammatory response, so fever may be the only sign. Patient may be hypothermic, confused, or hypotensive instead. Maintain a low threshold to treat.
Aetiology
Common Organisms
  • Commonest: Staph epidermidis (coagulase-negative Gram-positive) — usually from indwelling lines in cancer patients
  • Empirical cover must target Gram-negatives including Pseudomonas — this is why piperacillin-tazobactam (Tazocin) is chosen over narrow Gram-positive cover
Emergency Response — The Sequence
Antibiotics are NOT delayed for investigations — give Tazocin first, take cultures around it
StepActionNote
1IV piperacillin-tazobactam (Tazocin) immediatelyWithin 1 hour ("door-to-needle") — before cultures if needed
2Cultures + septic screenBlood (peripheral and line), FBC, CRP, U&E, LFT, clotting, lactate; CXR, urine/sputum/stool
348h reassessStill febrile/unwell → escalate: meropenem ± vancomycin (vancomycin if line infection/MRSA suspected)
44–6 days unresponsiveInvestigate fungal infection → antifungals (e.g. amphotericin)
De-escalation: switch to oral antibiotics once apyrexial for 48h; continue 10–14 days total

Prevention Strategy
  • Anticipated neutrophils <0.5 → fluoroquinolone prophylaxis (e.g. ciprofloxacin) during the expected nadir
  • G-CSF (filgrastim) — shortens duration of neutropenia in high-risk chemotherapy regimens
Exam Pearls
Neutrophils <0.5 + temp >38°C (or sepsis signs) on chemo = neutropenic sepsis — the definition is the diagnosis
Tazocin within 1 hour — do NOT wait for cultures or imaging
Signs may be blunted (no neutrophils → muted inflammation); treat on low threshold — beware hypothermia/confusion as the only signs
Commonest organism: Staph epidermidis (lines), but empirical cover targets Pseudomonas/Gram-negatives
Escalation ladder: Tazocin → meropenem ± vancomycin (48h) → antifungals (4–6 days)
Prophylaxis: fluoroquinolone ± G-CSF; cross-ref chemo complications (TLS, marrow failure)
HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria:
Malaria: Overview
Malaria = protozoan Plasmodium infection via female Anopheles mosquito

The returning-traveller fever — suspect in anyone with fever who lives in or has travelled to an endemic area
The decisive fork:
Falciparum — most severe, no dormant stage, RBC sequestration → complications (cerebral, AKI, DIC) → treat aggressively with IV artesunate

Vivax/Ovale — milder but relapsing — hypnozoites in liver → need primaquine for terminal cure
Protective host factors (cross-ref Sickle Cell): sickle-cell trait, G6PD deficiency, thalassaemia, HLA-B53, Duffy-negative (specifically blocks vivax)
Life Cycle
Step-by-Step
  • Mosquito injects sporozoites → liver (hepatocytes) → merozoites
  • vivax/ovale only: some hepatocytes form dormant hypnozoites → relapse weeks/months/years later
  • Hepatocyte ruptures → merozoites enter RBCs → replicate → rupture every 48h → haemolysis + pyrogen release → cyclical fever → more merozoites
  • Falciparum: infected RBCs adhere to small-vessel endothelium → sequestration/occlusion → cerebral malaria, AKI, etc.

FeatureFalciparumVivax / OvaleMalariae
SeverityMost severeMilderMild, chronic
Liver dormancyNoneHypnozoites → relapseNone
Fever patternIrregular/continuousTertian (48h)Quartan (72h)

Key riskSequestration → complicationsRelapseNephrotic syndrome (chronic)
Clinical Features
Symptoms
  • Fever, rigors, profuse sweating, malaise, myalgia, headache, vomiting
  • Signs: pallor (anaemia), hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice (haemolysis → bilirubin)
Falciparum Complications (Severe Branch)
  • Cerebral malaria (seizures, coma)
  • AKI — "blackwater fever" (haemoglobinuria)
  • Pulmonary oedema/ARDS
  • DIC (cross-ref DIC note)
  • Severe haemolytic anaemia
  • Hypoglycaemia — complication AND quinine side-effect (classic trap)
  • Multi-organ failure
Investigations
Blood Films (Gold Standard)
  • Thick film — detects/screens for parasites (sensitivity)
  • Thin film — identifies species + parasitaemia % (quantification)
  • 3 films over 3 days to exclude (48h cycle); high suspicion + negative → repeat at 12h and 24h
Additional
  • Rapid antigen tests (RDTs) — modern adjunct to film
  • Parasitaemia >2% = suggests severe disease
  • FBC (anaemia, thrombocytopenia), LFTs, glucose, clotting (DIC screen)
Management
Uncomplicated Malaria (Oral)
  • Artemether-lumefantrine (Riamet) — first-line
  • Atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone)
  • Quinine + doxycycline
Severe/Complicated Malaria
  • IV artesunate = treatment of choice (over IV quinine)
  • Admit all falciparum (risk of rapid deterioration)
  • IV artesunate for severe malaria — parasitaemia >10% is a severity marker (routine exchange transfusion no longer recommended)
Relapse Prevention (Vivax/Ovale)
  • Primaquine — clears hypnozoites from the liver (terminal prophylaxis)
  • Check G6PD status first — primaquine causes haemolysis in G6PD deficiency
Prophylaxis
  • Bite avoidance: nets, DEET, covering up
  • Chemoprophylaxis per region: Malarone / doxycycline / mefloquine

Falciparum = the killer — no relapse, but sequestration → cerebral malaria/AKI/DIC; admit all
Vivax/ovale relapse from hypnozoites → primaquine (check G6PD first — haemolysis risk)
Thick film = detect; thin film = speciate + quantify; 3 negatives over 3 days to exclude
IV artesunate = first-line in severe malaria (not IV quinine)
Tertian (48h) vivax/ovale · Quartan (72h) malariae · malariae → nephrotic syndrome
Protective: sickle trait, G6PD, thalassaemia, Duffy-negative (vivax) — cross-ref sickle cell · Parasitaemia >10% → severe malaria (IV artesunate; exchange transfusion no longer routine)
HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopenia:
Thrombocytopenia — Overview
The decisive fork: ↓ Production vs ↑ Destruction. Is the marrow failing to make platelets, or are they made but consumed/destroyed?
↓ Production (marrow fails)
Sepsis · B12/folate deficiency · Liver failure (↓thrombopoietin) · Leukaemia/MDS · Drugs (valproate, methotrexate, isotretinoin, antihistamines, PPIs) · Alcohol
Usually other cytopenias + abnormal marrow
↑ Destruction (platelets consumed)
ITP — immune (anti-GPIIb/IIIa) · TTP — microangiopathic (ADAMTS13↓) · HIT — immune (anti-PF4/heparin) · HUS — microangiopathic (Shiga toxin) · DIC — consumptive
Isolated low platelet count; normal/active marrow
Bleeding pattern: Thrombocytopenia → mucocutaneous/platelet-type bleeding — petechiae, purpura, epistaxis, gum bleeding, menorrhagia. (Deep joint/muscle bleeding = factor deficiency.)
Clinical Features by Count
Platelet countRisk

ITP (Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura)
Mechanism & Demographics
  • Anti-GPIIb/IIIa antibodies (usually IgG) → platelet destruction
  • Children: acute, post-viral, self-limiting
  • Adults: chronic, women; can be 2° to SLE / CLL / HIV
  • Isolated thrombocytopenia — clotting normal
Investigations
  • Isolated thrombocytopenia; antiplatelet antibodies
  • Bone marrow: ↑ megakaryocytes — do before steroids to exclude leukaemia
Management
  1. Oral prednisolone — 1st line
  2. IVIG — if urgent (pre-procedure / active bleed); raises count fast
  3. Splenectomy — if <30 after 3 months steroids
  4. TPO-receptor agonists (eltrombopag / romiplostim) or rituximab — later lines
TTP (Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura)
Mechanism: ADAMTS13 deficiency (inherited or autoimmune) → uncleaved vWF multimers → platelet microthrombi in small vessels → consumption (thrombocytopenia) + RBC shearing (MAHA)
Causes
  • Idiopathic, post-infection; SLE, HIV, tumours
  • Drugs: ciclosporin, OCP, clopidogrel, penicillin, aciclovir
Classic Pentad
  • Fever
  • Neurological signs
  • Thrombocytopenia
  • MAHA (microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia)
  • Renal failure
Management
  • Plasma exchange — urgent, first-line (replaces ADAMTS13)
  • Steroids + rituximab
  • NEVER transfuse platelets unless life-threatening bleed — fuels more thrombosis
HIT (Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia)
Mechanism: Anti-PF4/heparin antibodies → platelet activation → paradoxical thrombosis AND thrombocytopenia
Key Clinical Rules
  • Platelet fall typically 5–10 days after starting heparin
  • The timing is the diagnostic clue (4T score)
  • Paradoxical thrombosis, not just bleeding
Management
  • Stop heparin immediately
  • Switch to alternative anticoagulant: argatroban / fondaparinux / DOAC
  • NOT warfarin acutely
  • NOT platelet transfusion

Pancytopenia — Overview
Definition: Reduction in all three cell lines — anaemia + neutropenia/leucopenia + thrombocytopenia. It is a pattern, not a disease — the task is always to find the cause.
The decisive fork: Hypocellular marrow (production failure) vs Cellular marrow (ineffective / destruction / infiltration) — decided by bone marrow biopsy.

Fatigue, pallor, SOB

  • Viral (EBV, hepatitis, parvovirus)
  • Radiation

2. If true → EPO low (Primary / PV) vs EPO high (Secondary)

  2. Aspirin — antiplatelet

Malignant Spinal Cord Compression (MSCC)

Compression of the spinal cord or cauda equina by tumour — usually vertebral metastases. Commonest primaries: breast, lung, prostate, myeloma, renal.

🩺 Features
  • Back pain — often the first symptom; worse on lying flat, coughing or straining
  • Radicular pain, limb weakness, a sensory level
  • Bladder/bowel dysfunction (a late, ominous sign)
  • UMN signs below the level (LMN if cauda equina)
💊 Management
  • Urgent whole-spine MRI (within 24 h)
  • High-dose dexamethasone (e.g. 16 mg/day) + PPI cover
  • Definitive: surgical decompression or radiotherapy; involve the MSCC coordinator
  • Time-critical — treat before neurology becomes irreversible
New or progressive back pain in a patient with cancer is MSCC until proven otherwise.
Superior Vena Cava Obstruction (SVCO)

Obstruction of the SVC impairs venous return from the head, neck and upper limbs. Causes: lung cancer (especially small-cell), lymphoma, thymoma, mediastinal metastases; also central-line thrombosis.

🩺 Features
  • Swelling & plethora of the face, neck and arms; distended neck/chest wall veins
  • Dyspnoea, cough, headache (worse bending forward)
  • Pemberton’s sign: facial congestion/cyanosis on raising the arms
  • Severe: stridor/airway compromise, cerebral oedema
💊 Management
  • Sit up, high-flow oxygen; dexamethasone
  • CXR (mediastinal mass) then CT chest with contrast; tissue diagnosis where possible
  • Endovascular stenting for rapid relief (severe cases)
  • Radiotherapy / chemotherapy per tumour type (chemo for small-cell & lymphoma); anticoagulate if thrombotic
Tumour Lysis Syndrome (TLS)

Massive tumour-cell breakdown (usually within days of starting chemotherapy, occasionally spontaneous) releases intracellular contents and causes acute metabolic derangement → AKI, arrhythmia, seizures.

🧪 Biochemistry
  • ↑ Potassium (arrhythmia risk)
  • ↑ Phosphate
  • ↑ Urate (uric acid)
  • ↓ Calcium (binds the raised phosphate)
⚠️ Who is at risk
  • High-grade lymphoma (Burkitt’s), acute leukaemias (ALL/AML)
  • Bulky, chemosensitive tumours; high white-cell count
  • Pre-existing renal impairment / dehydration
💊 Prevention & treatment
  • IV hydration + close monitoring of U&E, urate, phosphate, calcium; cardiac monitoring
  • Allopurinol for prophylaxis in lower-risk patients
  • Rasburicase (recombinant urate oxidase) for high risk/established TLS — contraindicated in G6PD deficiency
  • Treat hyperkalaemia; manage AKI (dialysis if needed)
Hypercalcaemia of Malignancy

The commonest life-threatening metabolic complication of cancer. Mechanisms: PTHrP (squamous-cell lung, breast, renal), osteolytic bone metastases (breast, myeloma), and tumour 1,25-vitamin D (lymphoma).

🩺 Features — “stones, bones, groans, moans, thrones”
  • Polyuria, polydipsia, dehydration
  • Constipation, abdominal pain, nausea
  • Confusion, lethargy, low mood
  • Bone pain, renal stones; short QT, arrhythmia
💊 Management
  • Aggressive IV fluids (0.9% saline) first — rehydrate and promote calcium excretion
  • IV bisphosphonate (e.g. zoledronic acid) once rehydrated
  • Denosumab if bisphosphonate-refractory / renal impairment; steroids for lymphoma-related
  • Treat the underlying malignancy
See also Hyperparathyroidism / Hypercalcaemia (Endocrinology) for the full differential and work-up.
Exam Pearls
Neutropenic sepsis
IV piperacillin–tazobactam within 1 hour of presentation — never wait for the neutrophil count.
Spinal cord compression
Back pain + neurology in a cancer patient → urgent whole-spine MRI + high-dose dexamethasone.
SVCO
Facial/arm swelling, distended veins, dyspnoea; small-cell lung cancer; Pemberton’s sign; stenting for rapid relief.
Tumour lysis biochemistry
↑K, ↑phosphate, ↑urate, ↓calcium. Prevent with hydration + allopurinol; treat with rasburicase (avoid in G6PD deficiency).
Highest TLS risk
Burkitt’s lymphoma and acute leukaemias with a high white-cell count.
Malignant hypercalcaemia
Fluids first, then a bisphosphonate. Commonly PTHrP-mediated (squamous lung) or myeloma bone disease.
